passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Correction That Was Not Read

emails.subject: Correction published 3 October — placement
emails.body:
Dear Editor,

On 26 September the Gazette reported that my restaurant had been "closed following an inspection". The inspection took place and we passed it. We closed for four days for a scheduled kitchen refit that had been booked since July.

You published a correction on 3 October and I want to acknowledge that it was accurate, prompt and unreserved. I have no complaint about its wording.

My complaint is where it sat. The original was the second item on your homepage for two days and was shared 340 times from your own account. The correction is a paragraph on a corrections page that is reached from a link in the footer, and it was not posted to social media at all. I checked; the account posted eleven times on 3 October and none of them was this.

I have had four cancellations since, and two callers mentioned the closure. Neither had seen the correction. I do not think that is because they were careless.

I am not asking for compensation and I am not asking you to grovel. I am asking that a correction travel by the same route as the error. If a story went on the homepage and to social media, its correction should go to both. If that is not your policy, I would like to know that it is not, so I can stop assuming it is.

Sincerely,
Oyelaran Adebayo

emails.subject: RE: Correction published 3 October — placement
emails.body:
Dear Mr Adebayo,

It is not our policy, and you are right that it should be. I am not going to claim it was an oversight in your case when it is simply how we have always done it.

Corrections here go to the corrections page because that is where corrections have gone since the paper was printed on paper, and nobody revisited the practice when the traffic moved. The result is that our errors reach an audience and our corrections reach the people who go looking for them, which is close to nobody. That is a real asymmetry and it is ours.

From Monday: any correction to a story that appeared on the homepage runs on the homepage for the same number of days the original did. Any correction to a story we posted socially is posted socially from the same account. Your correction goes up under that rule today, and the social post will go out this afternoon.

On the four cancellations, I am not going to offer you compensation because I do not think I can establish the connection and I would rather not pretend I can. What I can do is put the correction where people will actually see it, which is what you asked for.

One thing I should say plainly. The original reporter did contact you before publication and did not reach you, and then filed anyway. That is the actual failure — the placement of the correction made it worse, but the story should not have run. I have said so internally and I am saying it to you.

Regards,
Hester Vandenberg
Editor

passages.title: What Disappears When a Local Paper Closes
passages.content:
The closure of local newspapers is usually reported as a business story, and the loss described in terms of jobs and civic sentiment. Research into what happens afterwards suggests the effects are more specific, more measurable and stranger than the sentimental account implies.

The clearest documented consequence is financial rather than cultural. Studies of municipalities that lost their local paper find borrowing costs rise afterwards, because the routine scrutiny that came free with a reporter attending council meetings is priced into lending once it disappears. Nobody set out to buy oversight; it was a side effect of somebody being in the room, and its absence turns out to have a number attached.

Coverage does not vanish evenly, which is the second finding. National and regional outlets continue to cover the dramatic — a scandal, a disaster, an election. What disappears is the undramatic and continuous: planning applications, licensing decisions, procurement, the committee meeting where a budget line changes. This is precisely the material that is boring on any given day and consequential over years, and its absence is invisible because nobody misses a story that was never written.

The replacement is partial and uneven. Community social media groups and volunteer newsletters do fill some of the gap, and they are genuinely useful for immediate, local and practical information. They rarely reproduce the specific function that was lost, which is a person with time, a press card and a habit of attending things that nobody else attends. Volunteers cover what interests them; a reporter covered what was on the agenda.

There is also a documented effect on what people know about their own area. In communities without a local outlet, residents are less able to name their elected representatives and more likely to rely on national framing for local questions — which tends to import national divisions into decisions that had none. Local political contests become less distinguishable from national ones, and turnout in local elections falls.

None of this establishes that the previous model was sustainable, and nostalgia is not a business plan. It does suggest that what is being lost is not mainly sentiment or employment, but a specific and quantifiable form of routine attention, and that anything designed to replace it should be judged on whether it attends the boring meetings.

passages.title: Should Public Money Fund Local Journalism?

viewpoints.name: Councillor Nils Bergström
viewpoints.text: I voted for a local news fund and I am aware of the obvious objection, which is that I am voting to fund people whose job is to scrutinise me. I would rather name that than let someone else. The safeguard we used is that allocation is decided by an independent panel with no council members, on criteria set in advance and published. Whether that is sufficient I genuinely do not know — it has run for two years and nobody has tested it with an uncomfortable story yet. Ask me again when they do.

viewpoints.name: Marguerite Boileau, editor
viewpoints.text: I run a paper that would benefit and I have not applied. My reason is narrow and I do not expect others to share it: the moment I take the money, every story I write about that council is read differently by my readers, whether or not it should be. Perception is part of the product I sell. I would support a fund structured so the money never comes from the body being covered — national rather than municipal, or from a levy the council does not administer — and I would apply to that one tomorrow.

viewpoints.name: Dr Anwar Haddad, media researcher
viewpoints.text: The evidence on public funding is better than critics assume and narrower than advocates claim. Where independence is structurally protected — arm's-length allocation, multi-year settlements, no discretionary renewal — outlets are not measurably less critical of their funders. Where funding is annual and discretionary, they are. That is not a finding about journalists' integrity; it is a finding about incentives, and it means the design matters far more than whether the money is public or private.

viewpoints.name: Tessa Ohanian, community newsletter volunteer
viewpoints.text: Every scheme I have seen is built for organisations with a constitution, audited accounts and someone to write the application. I produce a newsletter for four thousand households from my kitchen table and I have never been eligible for anything, because eligibility is designed around the thing that already failed rather than the thing that replaced it. I am not asking for a grant. I am asking why the criteria assume the future of local news looks like its past.
